source.version_note: AI & SOCIETY 41:6893–6908, published online 24 March 2026; supplied article is labelled REVIEW despite reporting original survey analysis.
source.verification_method: All sixteen supplied pages read. Tables 3–6 on page 9 and data-availability/bibliography on page 15 visually checked. Several cited-source metadata records verified independently, without claiming their full texts read.

citation.title: Artificial intelligence as a moral mediator: emotional reciprocity driving happiness in hospitality

reading.source_scope_note: Definitions and a cross-sectional hotel survey model are documented separately. Major internal reporting inconsistencies, overlapping indicators and unavailable raw data limit reliance on the empirical claims. Associations do not establish AI-induced happiness, necessity of AI mediation, actual privacy protection or autonomous moral agency.
access_limits: All sixteen pages read, with key tables and the contradictory data statement visually verified.
No raw data, item-level questionnaire, analysis project, cluster handling, measurement-invariance output or direct-effect-to-happiness results were available in the supplied file.
Crossref/PMLR metadata checks concern identity, authors, venue and dates only. Cited emotional-labor, psychological-safety and leadership primary works and books are not counted as fully read.

study.sample: Reports an email invitation to managers at 1,200 Ecostars-registry hotels in Spain, with 49 hotels/787 employees responding and 42 hotels/754 employees retained. Abstract also identifies 42 managers. Exact pooled analysis denominator and role/cluster handling are not clearly specified.
study.qualitative_component: Two managerial focus groups develop/refine the model. Section 2 describes the first group as 42 managers representing 754 employees, whereas Section 4.3 describes managers from 11 randomly selected hotels. Group sizes, overlap, timing and qualitative analytic procedure need clarification.
study.design: Cross-sectional seven-point self-report survey. Six proposed constructs: emotional labor sustainability, ethical AI governance, human-centered leadership, shared prosperity, AI-mediated emotional reciprocity and workplace happiness. No random assignment, before/after comparison or no-AI control.
study.technology: Organizations reportedly used workforce analytics, scheduling, dashboards and sentiment/feedback tools for at least a year. No named system, technical validation, objective emotion accuracy, usage log or independent privacy/performance audit is supplied.
study.measurement: Initial 29 indicators become 24 proposed items, then Table 2 retains 17. Leadership and happiness each retain two. Happiness includes sustainable emotional well-being/psychological safety and recognized/recoverable/fairly allocated emotional labor, overlapping predictor content.
study.model: SmartPLS 4.1.0.3. Seven reported direct paths end in shared prosperity → AI-MER → happiness; the only direct incoming path to happiness shown is AI-MER. Reported AI-MER→WH beta=.641, SP→AI-MER=.709, WH R²=.411 and AI-MER R²=.503 describe the fitted association model, not intervention effects.
study.multigroup: Manager/employee path estimates are shown with separate significance tests. No explicit between-group difference test or measurement-invariance result is reported here. Several manager indirect paths in Table 9 are nonsignificant despite broad mediation claims.
study.reliability_alert: The data-availability statement says no datasets were generated or analysed, contradicting the described data collection, SmartPLS analysis and author-contribution statement. This unresolved inconsistency prevents independent confirmation; it is not by itself proof of fabrication.

summary: Add emotional labor, emotional reciprocity and psychological safety as explicitly scoped human processes/conditions. Preserve definitions while attaching major limits to the survey's empirical claims. Do not manufacture new proven AI mechanisms from each variable in the proposed governance model.

findings.definition: The emotional effort involved in meeting the interpersonal expectations of a work role.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Explicit human-work construct discussed and represented through perceived organizational sustainability items; no causal test of AI's effect on actual emotional effort
findings.ai_proposal: Assess whether AI-assisted service workflows reduce or redistribute human emotional demands through voluntary worker reports and workload outcomes. Evaluate generated service tone as an observable requirement without claiming the model feels exhaustion. Preserve human oversight, proportionate data collection and the ability to contest workload decisions.
findings.novelty_rationale: Work-role emotional demands differ from emotion regulation generally, contagious affect or emotional reasoning. The article explicitly describes employees as producers of emotional labor and treats emotional effort as a bounded work resource.

evidence.quote: Hospitality work is saturated with emotional effort
Service expectations are bounded to avoid normalizing silent emotional sacrifice

findings.evidence_scope: The article defines emotional labor sustainability and includes items about recognized effort, recovery, bounded expectations and workload design. It does not directly measure felt emotion, display regulation, actual service episodes, burnout incidence or changes caused by AI. Hochschild/Grandey and scale-development works are secondary references here.
findings.boundary: Emotional work can be appropriate, meaningful and consensual; it is not inherently exploitation, insincerity or burnout. Human emotional effort, displayed friendliness and an AI's generated tone differ. No model exhaustion, diagnosis or justification for intrusive emotion surveillance follows from this concept.

findings.definition: A mutual exchange of care, warmth and empathic responses in an interaction.
findings.origin: Interpersonal and organizational psychology / hospitality relationships
findings.ai_evidence_status: Explicitly defined interpersonal process; the study's AI-mediated scale measures perceived governance/redistribution rather than directly observed reciprocal emotion
findings.ai_proposal: Separate a person's perceived emotional acknowledgment from actual two-way human relationships and an AI's generated supportive responses. Test whether AI-mediated employee/guest feedback supports appropriate recognition without implying the model feels care, requiring emotional repayment or exploiting attachment.
findings.novelty_rationale: A relational exchange of emotional acknowledgment differs from an obligation to repay a benefit, reputation-based indirect reciprocity, or merely catching another person's affect. The article's later AI-MER construct is a specific organizational operationalization, not an exact synonym for all reciprocity.

evidence.quote: care, warmth, and empathy between employees and guests.

findings.evidence_scope: The introduction explicitly defines emotional reciprocity. The empirical AI-MER items concern aggregated indicators, task redistribution, human supervision and service interactions, so the path coefficients cannot be treated as direct measurements of mutual felt care or actual AI emotion.
findings.boundary: Reciprocity need not be equal, immediate, compelled or emotionally identical. A supportive AI response is not proof of felt mutuality or a relationship with duties of emotional repayment. Do not confuse care, conformity, contagion, flattery and fair institutional treatment.

findings.definition: A shared sense that people can speak up or raise concerns at work without fear of reprisal.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Explicit secondary concept linked to Edmondson 1999; embedded in compound leadership/happiness indicators, not independently measured or causally tested here
findings.ai_proposal: Assess whether people can question AI recommendations, report errors or contest workplace decisions without retaliation. Measure that climate separately from satisfaction, system accuracy and the existence of a feedback button. Do not describe a model as feeling socially safe or equate agreeable responses with safe oversight.
findings.novelty_rationale: A climate for interpersonal speaking up differs from technical safety, subjective proximity, comfort, universal agreement or willingness to obey. The article gives a clear fear-of-reprisal description, but its cited original scale remains unread.

evidence.quote: empowers employees to voice concerns and innovate without
Employees experience sustained emotional well-being and psychological safety collectively

findings.evidence_scope: Psychological safety is explained conceptually and appears inside compound items. There is no separate validated safety scale, observed speaking-up behavior or randomized management/AI intervention. This paper is a secondary conceptual source, not an independent replication of Edmondson's primary findings.
findings.boundary: Psychological safety does not mean freedom from justified accountability, absence of disagreement or guaranteed physical/technical safety. A pleasant tone or a positive happiness score is insufficient evidence that workers can challenge authority without retaliation. It describes human perceptions and institutions, not a model's felt vulnerability.

findings.term: Organizational emotional-labor support is distinct from identified emotion regulation
findings.definition: Workload recognition, recovery and redistribution can support people's emotional demands without establishing a particular internal regulation process or its improvement.
findings.novelty_rationale: A boundary within the existing regulation concept; the survey measures perceived institutional practice rather than individuals' specific emotion-regulation strategies.

evidence.quote: employees’ perceptions of organizational ethical practices

findings.evidence_scope: The framework proposes reducing overload through task allocation, breaks and care responses. No surface/deep-acting, reappraisal, suppression, affect dynamics or intervention benefit is directly tested. This note does not fill an emotion-regulation primary-paper gap.
findings.boundary: Institutional support, perceived fairness, emotional display and actual affect modulation should be separately measured. A model recommendation is not evidence of felt regulation or of a beneficial human outcome.

findings.term: Emotional visibility can support recognition or enable instrumentalization
findings.definition: Making workers' emotional effort visible can enable support but can also encourage control or assessment that disregards their autonomy and legitimate interests.
findings.novelty_rationale: A governance boundary, not proof that all analytics or emotional labor necessarily instrumentalize people.

evidence.quote: AI systems can intensify control, reduce autonomy, and
produce performative compliance, autonomy reduction, or

findings.evidence_scope: The article explicitly discusses surveillance, power and autonomy risks while studying positively framed perceptions. It does not independently measure actual surveillance, consent quality, discriminatory assessment or performative compliance. The proposed risks are not observed effect estimates.
findings.boundary: Consensual, proportionate support differs from exploitative control. Aggregation alone does not prove anonymity or eliminate profiling and reidentification risk. A perceived ethical-governance score cannot certify privacy, fairness or legal compliance.

methodological_limits: The cross-sectional self-report design establishes associations among perceptions, not temporal order, causal mediation, intervention efficacy or necessary conditions for happiness. The authors acknowledge this but elsewhere claim a clear causal pathway and that happiness would not arise without AI-MER.

The page-15 data-availability statement says no datasets were generated or analysed, while methods/results and author contributions describe collecting and analyzing survey data. This visually confirmed contradiction is unresolved. It is a reporting/reproducibility concern, not by itself evidence of fabricated data.

No unaided/no-AI group or predeployment baseline isolates AI's contribution. All selected organizations reportedly use AI, so the article cannot show that AI is necessary or superior to equivalent human-led support.

The sample is clustered within 42 retained hotels, but cluster-aware standard errors, multilevel structure and bootstrap unit are not specified. Treating all employee responses as independent could affect uncertainty; original output is needed to determine the handling.

The abstract identifies 754 employees and 42 managers, but the pooled model denominator, survey routing and manager-versus-hotel counts need clarification. The Ecostars registry and voluntary response select a particular organizational context; random sampling does not make nonresponse random.

Seven hotels and 33 employee cases are removed through unspecified rigorous screening/consistency checks. The article does not sufficiently report exclusion rules, missing-data handling, dates or attrition by group.

The first focus group is described as 42 managers in Section 2 and as managers from 11 hotels in Section 4.3. The two groups' sizes, overlap and analytic procedure are not reconciled. Manager-defined indicators can miss frontline concerns, as the authors acknowledge.

Initial 29 indicators become 24 and then 17 retained items. The prose lists AI-MER43 as a low-loading item, while Table 2 omits AI-MER3 and retains ELS4 with loading .689 despite the stated .70 threshold. Do not guess whether this is a label or retention error.

HCL and WH are reduced to two indicators each. Internal consistency and AVE do not establish broad content validity, especially when happiness overlaps with psychological safety and predictor-like emotional-labor conditions.

WH2 directly concerns recognized, recoverable and fairly allocated emotional labor, overlapping ELS and fairness constructs. Theoretical distinctness by functional level does not alone resolve shared wording, common-source effects or criterion contamination.

Tables 4 and 5 appear to have reversed discriminant-validity labels. Table 5's diagonal equals the square roots of Table 3 AVE and its off-diagonal entries match the model correlations, although captioned HTMT. Table 4 lacks diagonals and resembles HTMT, although captioned Fornell–Larcker. This is visually verified; original SmartPLS output is needed before silently swapping or declaring validity established.

The text claims all HTMT values fall below .90, but Table 5's diagonal includes .920 because it appears to contain square-root AVE instead. Do not treat those diagonal entries as failed HTMT tests or assume the captions are correct.

A sentence claims validity for transformational leadership at group and individual levels although the model concerns human-centered leadership and no corresponding multilevel validation is reported. This looks inconsistent with the described constructs and needs clarification.

SRMR is described with a .08 threshold, but no actual SRMR value is reported. Positive Q²predict values alone do not establish external validity or practical benefit; folds, baselines and prediction errors are not developed here.

Figure 1 and Tables 7–8 show AI-MER as the only direct predictor of WH. The later statement that direct ELS/EAIG/HCL/SP→WH effects are largely nonsignificant is not supported by presented estimates. Omitting those paths structurally is not evidence of full mediation.

Table 9 includes nonsignificant manager indirect paths, including EAIG→SP→AI-MER→WH p=.102 and ELS→EAIG→SP→AI-MER→WH p=.136. Broad statements of complete, robust mediation across paths overstate the displayed results.

Different coefficients or different within-group p values do not establish manager–employee differences. No explicit difference-test p values or measurement-invariance analysis are given, and the manager group is much smaller.
The text at one point labels beta .457/.400 as SP→AI-MER, but these are the indirect SP→AI-MER→WH estimates; direct coefficients are .716/.601. Distinguish direct from indirect paths.
T-statistic formatting inconsistently uses commas or omits decimal separators. The prose clarifies some values; do not interpret 7785 as an actual t of seven thousand or p=.000 as exact zero.

AI is alternately said not to have autonomous moral agency and to be a structural ethical agent or moral agent. Operational mediation within human governance must be distinguished from intrinsic moral cognition. The survey does not adjudicate universal machine capacities.

Emotional reciprocity shifts from interpersonal care exchange to an organizational AI-MER composite and later to employee receptiveness to interventions. These are not interchangeable operational definitions; favorable governance perceptions do not directly show mutual emotion.

Items assert no profiling/surveillance risks and positive care outcomes. Agreement with such statements is not a technical audit or evidence that emotion inference is accurate, consent is freely given or burnout was prevented.

No validated burnout diagnosis, emotion-regulation strategy measure, actual workload change, guest satisfaction outcome or retention follow-up is reported. Proposed management benefits are recommendations, not demonstrated improvements.

cross_paper_learning.finding: A cross-sectional serial path model cannot establish a causal psychological chain. Overlapping predictors/outcomes, modified scales and subgroup claims require independent scrutiny before interpreting significant paths as mechanisms.
A statistically significant indirect association need not explain the hypothesized effect. Here, omitted direct paths also cannot establish full mediation or that AI is necessary.

Relational language about machines should distinguish observable organizational roles from felt reciprocity, attributed standing and actual moral agency. This paper's competing agent/mechanism descriptions do not settle machine experience.

deferred.reason: Retain as the paper's proposed organizational composite, with its four indicators and limits, rather than another independently established behavioral mechanism.

Important human occupational construct, but not independently defined or measured with a burnout instrument here. Seek a primary definition/measurement paper rather than infer a diagnosis from emotional workload.
Relevant primary emotional-labor literature is cited, but these distinct processes are not defined or measured in the supplied paper. Do not claim extraction or full reading of the cited originals.
A proposed benefit, not a causally established new behavior; no no-AI control, randomized intervention or temporal evidence.
Explicitly acknowledged risk, not an observed causal effect or new validated syndrome in this study.

limitations: Three human concepts added with limited/conceptual evidence scope. Major source-reporting contradictions are recorded transparently; no fabricated statistical repair, source quota, annual counts or ethical edges.
